{{Short description|American physicist (1920–1993)}}
[[File:ChicagoPileTeam.png|thumb|The [[Chicago Pile-1|Chicago Pile]] team in 1946; Lichtenberger is in the middle row, third from the left.]]

'''Harold V. Lichtenberger''' (April 22, 1920 – December 7, 1993) was an American physicist who was involved in the planning of the [[Chicago Pile-1]], the first [[nuclear reactor]] to achieve [[Criticality (status)|criticality]], and in other reactor experiments at the [[Argonne National Laboratory]].

== Life ==
Lichtenberger was born in [[Decatur, Illinois]]. He graduated from [[Millikin University]] with a bachelor's degree in 1942. During the construction of the Chicago Pile-1, he was part of the team measuring materials,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/History-of-Argonne-Reactor-Operations.pdf |title=History of Argonne Reactor Operations |publisher=[[Argonne National Laboratory]] |page=4 |date=n.d.}}</ref> and during testing he, Warren Nyer and [[Alvin C. Graves]] made up a "suicide squadron" known as the liquid-control squad: if the [[control rods]] failed, they were to pour a solution of [[cadmium]] salts over the reactor to absorb [[neutron]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://energy.gov/sites/prod/files/The%20First%20Reactor.pdf |author1-first=Corbin |author1-last=Allardice |author2-first=Edward R. |author2-last=Trapnell |journal=The First Reactor |title=The First Pile |publisher=US Department of Energy |date=1982 |page=23 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author1-first=Corbin |author1-last=Allardice |author2-first=Edward R. |author2-last=Trapnell |title=When we Turned on the Atom |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1298&dat=19671127&id=v81NAAAAIBAJ&sjid=RooDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5713,3820821&hl=en |newspaper=[[The Free Lance-Star]] |location=Fredericksburg, Virginia |date=November 27, 1967 |page=6 }}</ref> He was then responsible, with [[Albert Nobles]], for reassembling the reactor after it was disassembled and moved to the Metallurgical Laboratory's more remote [[Site A]] location outside Chicago.<ref>"History of Argonne Reactor Operations", p. 6.</ref>

With [[Albert Wattenberg]], Lichtenberger designed and tested the first [[pressurized heavy-water reactor]], [[Chicago Pile-3]],<ref name=bio>{{cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/cp1-pioneers/ |title=The Chicago Pile 1 Pioneers |publisher=Argonne National Laboratory |date=February 18, 2016 }}</ref> and with [[Walter Zinn]] performed a number of other reactor experiments at the Argonne National Laboratory, including the first [[breeder reactor]], [[EBR-1]], and the [[boiling water reactor]] [[BORAX]]-III, the first reactor to supply power to an entire city ([[Arco, Idaho]], in 1955 with 500&nbsp;kW).<ref name=bio/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/borax3/index.shtml |title=AEC Press release for BORAX-III lighting Arco, Idaho |author=US Atomic Energy Commission |via=Argonne National Laboratory |date=August 12, 1955 }}</ref> He became director of the Idaho Division of the [[Metallurgical Laboratory]] and Argonne National Laboratory, where new reactors were tested.

In 1954, Lichtenberger was also in charge of experiments at the proving ground in Idaho in which experimental reactors were systematically taken beyond criticality and caused to explode by manipulation of the control rods.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.castor.de/technik/atomkraft/1_1956/28.html |first=Robert |last=Gerwin |authorlink=Robert Gerwin |title=Keine Angst vor Atommeilern |work=Hobby |issue=1 |date=January 1956 |language=German |access-date=2016-05-17 |archive-date=2014-12-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141229000434/http://www.castor.de/technik/atomkraft/1_1956/28.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He died in [[West Simsbury, Connecticut]], in December 1993, of stomach cancer.<ref name=bio/>
